author: TEDx Talks
description:
When you ask people what they want to work on, anger management is consistently top of the list. The most common misconception is that venting or engaging in physical activity is the best self-regulatory strategy. However, research shows that these activities actually increase anger by raising arousal levels; instead, the most effective approach is to stop, drop, and roll: to pause, calm your body, and move forward with your day with a clearer mindset.

A professor in the school of communication, Dr. Brad J. Bushman has studied aggression and violence for over 30 years. He was a previously a member of President Obama’s committee on gun violence, and has testified before the U.S. Congress on the topic of youth violence. 

This talk was given at a TEDx event using the TED conference format but independently organized by a local community. Learn more at https://www.ted.com/tedx
title: Anger management: What works and what doesn’t | Brad Bushman | TEDxOhioStateUniversity

This speech is about how it is normal for high school students to feel unsure about their future. It explains how trying new things, even when you are not prepared, can help you discover what you enjoy and who you want to become. Through a personal experience with a school musical and the example of Nelson Mandela, the speech shows that not knowing is not the same as failing. The main message is that you do not need to have your whole life planned out—you just need to keep moving forward. Jacky Lin is a 14-year-old high school student with a strong passion for media, photography, and cinematography. He enjoys creating video edits and is actively involved in multiple film-based clubs, where he contributes to community projects, including filming for the school’s marketing department. Jacky also works on his own projects, such as filming school events and competitions, and creating edits that help highlight others and bring more recognition to people within the school community.

Drawing on personal family experience with her great-grandmother and the reality of global ageing populations, Angel unpacks real‑world BCI breakthroughs both internationally and within China. She paints a hopeful vision: using thought‑controlled technology, AI and humanoid robotics to give speech, independence and dignity back to elders living with stroke, injury or cognitive decline. This speech is not about futuristic gadgets — it is about preserving human‑to‑human love and connection, even when words can no longer be spoken. Angel Cheng is a sixth-grade IB learner with a huge heart and an even stronger sense of justice. She cares deeply about people whose voices are often overlooked—especially elderly individuals who have faced hardships early in life. description: The speech discusses how the finish line can be a motivation, but it can also be a danger — it can prevent people from ever seeing clearly what they have already achieved. William Jia isn’t your typical 12-year-old. A middle schooler with a passion for Jiu-Jitsu, debate, and science, he’s constantly pushing himself to grow—both mentally and physically. Through his TEDx talk, William shares a powerful personal experience that reshaped how he thinks about goals. He challenges the way we define success, uncovering the hidden impacts of what we strive for. By reflecting on his own journey, William invites others to rethink not just how they pursue their goals—but why they set them in the first place. description: What remains unchanged when life constantly asks us to evolve? Told by adults that acting and modelling were not meant for a girl like her, Sushmita Singh went on to win an international teen pageant at 18. She went on to work in television before leaving a long-running show in 2022 to compete in Miss India, and later represented India at the Miss United Continents pageant. In this inspiring talk, she reflects on resilience, self-belief, and the power of staying true to your core values as you navigate change, challenges, and new opportunities. Sushmita Singh is a boundary-pushing storyteller, and a dynamic creative force shaping modern cinema. Renowned for her fierce versatility and magnetic screen presence, she fearlessly uses her art to shatter stereotypes and spark vital conversations. description: In this powerful and engaging talk, Ylvie explores the hidden and visible costs of being a woman, from the ‘pink tax’ on everyday products to the unequal burden of maternity leave, menstrual stigma, and the devaluation of women’s bodies and labour. Blending personal experience with global examples, she shows how gender inequality is built into both culture and systems, shaping women’s lives from childhood onward. At the same time, she highlights progress, resilience, and the women throughout history who have fought for change. Ultimately, she calls on her audience to challenge these injustices and help build a world in which women are valued fully and equally. Ylvie Schraffanek is a Year 11 student who joined Lanna International School in Year 9. She is very active in the student-led public speaking programme, including debate, MUN, and mock trial, and she has frequently undertaken leadership roles. description: In this empowering and personal talk, Yardha reflects on her experiences in sport to challenge the idea that strength, power, and competitiveness belong mainly to men. Drawing on childhood memories, training experiences, and cultural expectations, she explores how gender stereotypes are learned rather than natural, and how they shape the way girls and women are seen, praised, and limited. She argues that the problem is not female strength itself, but a system that questions who is allowed to possess and display it. Ultimately, she calls on her audience to reject these expectations and embrace strength in all its forms. Yardhamarnee ‘Yardha’ Kuttig is a Year 11 student who has studied at Lanna International School for eleven years and is now in the final year of her IGCSE courses. description:
What if the stress you’re trying to escape is actually part of what makes life meaningful?

In a world obsessed with effortless success and perfect life plans, Abdur Rakib challenges us to rethink our relationship with struggle. From university admissions to early career challenges, he explores how obstacles can give our achievements greater meaning - and why a trouble-free life may not be the goal we think it is.

Rather than complicated frameworks and endless planning, Rakib offers a simple five-year, pen-and-paper approach to navigating major life transitions, financial milestones, and personal growth without losing sight of the journey itself. Abdur Rakib is a technology leader and entrepreneur serving as the Chief Operating Officer (COO) of Programming Hero and Phitron.io. With more than a decade of experience across software engineering, project management, strategy, and technology-driven organizations, he has built his career at the intersection of technology and people.

description: In this compelling and deeply personal talk, William reflects on his experience of racism and bullying as an international student in Canada, using it to question how schools teach, or fail to teach, global understanding. He argues that ignorance and stereotyping are often rooted in narrow, localised curricula that leave students with little knowledge of the wider world. Blending personal stories with a broader critique of education, he calls for schools to move beyond surface-level multiculturalism and embrace truly global learning. Ultimately, his speech is a powerful plea for education that builds empathy, challenges prejudice, and helps students see the person beyond the stereotype. William Wang is a Year 11 student who has studied at Lanna International School since Year 5. description: In this heartfelt and reflective talk, Alika challenges the pressure schools place on young people to fit in, arguing that education should nurture individuality rather than conformity. Through vivid personal memories of loneliness, self-doubt, and attempts to meet narrow expectations, she explores how school systems often reward sameness while overlooking different kinds of intelligence, creativity, and potential. She makes the case that students should not be defined by grades, popularity, or how well they match a social mould. Ultimately, she calls for schools to become places where students feel safe being fully themselves and learn to belong in their own skin. Alika Dahnpitak is a Year 11 student who joined Lanna International School in Year 8. Tracing a journey from childhood faith in fairness to a more critical understanding of global politics, she explores how institutions such as the UN, ICC, and ICJ help define moral standards around war crimes and human rights, yet often lack the enforcement needed to hold powerful actors accountable. While acknowledging these flaws, she argues that international law still shapes our collective conscience and can inspire citizens to demand stronger action and a more just world. Anita Bergin is a Year 11 student who has studied at Lanna International School for eight years. description: Quanto de quem somos ainda permanece no escuro? Uma pergunta aparentemente simples — What do I stand for? — fez Ana Cardoso perceber que, apesar de uma trajetória de realizações, havia partes de si mesma que ela ainda não conhecia. A partir da imagem de uma casa escura que, quando iluminada, revela-se uma enorme mansão, Ana reflete sobre potencial humano, escolhas e transformação. Perguntas que nos desconcertam, limitações inesperadas e encontros com outras pessoas podem abrir portas para espaços de nós mesmos que ainda não havíamos explorado. Um convite para acender as luzes da nossa própria casa — e ajudar outras pessoas a fazerem o mesmo. Ana Cardoso atua com desenvolvimento humano e liderança, depois de uma trajetória de 15 anos no mundo corporativo e de experiências profissionais e pessoais em diferentes países. description:
What do you really know about the food on your plate?

Umme Kulsum Popy challenges us to rethink agriculture - not simply as a profession, but as the foundation of our everyday lives. Drawing from her experience as an entrepreneur, she explores how food choices, harvesting practices, technology, and self-learning can shape the way we protect our health and understand the food system.

From encouraging young people to see agriculture as an opportunity to questioning what we consume, Popy makes a simple case: we cannot build a healthy future without understanding where our food comes from. Umme Kulsum Popy is an agriculture entrepreneur and advocate for food awareness and sustainable agricultural practices in Bangladesh. Through her work and digital engagement, she seeks to change how people perceive agriculture and encourage greater awareness of the food we consume.

Popy believes agriculture is not merely a traditional profession; it is a vital part of human life and an emerging space
title: The Food on Your Plate: Rethinking Agriculture and What We Eat | Umme Kulsum Popy | TEDxSUST

description:
A partir de sua experiência entre Brasil e Argentina, Helena O’Donnell reflete sobre as diferentes formas como os dois países lidaram com a memória das ditaduras militares. Enquanto a Argentina avançou na responsabilização e punição de agentes da repressão, o Brasil adotou, com a Lei da Anistia, uma política que dificultou a responsabilização dos responsáveis por graves violações de direitos humanos.

A palestra discute como essas escolhas distintas no tratamento do passado influenciam a maneira como as sociedades constroem sua memória histórica e enfrentam o presente. No caso brasileiro, a permanência de uma memória marcada pela impunidade e pela insuficiente responsabilização contribuiu para a fragilidade da cultura democrática e para a persistência de discursos e movimentos de caráter antidemocrático. A partir desse contexto, Helena questiona qual é o papel da juventude na preservação da memória e na construção de uma sociedade comprometida com a democracia. Helena O’Donnell é estu
title: O passado que insiste em ser futuro⁠ | Helena O’Donnell | TEDxEscola Parque Youth

In this personal and thought provoking talk, Kyanatha Azzahra explores the overlooked efforts of family, friends, teachers and others who quietly support us on our journey toward achievement.

description: We know we should exercise, save, sleep well and control our anger, yet we rarely act on what we know. Drawing on more than three decades in the pharmaceutical industry and on taking up strength training and mountaineering in his fifties, Madhusudan Rao argues that most of us do not face a knowledge problem but an execution problem. He explains why knowing costs nothing while doing demands effort, why motivation fades while routine endures, and why lasting change is usually boring. He leaves the audience with one question: what do you already know, but still don't do? A veteran corporate leader and operator, Madhusudan Rao brings decades of high-impact executive experience across India's healthcare and pharmaceutical ecosystems to his role as Partner at PedalStart. By merging raw ambition with proven real-world perspective, he helps the startup ecosystem build, fund, and scale with absolute confidence. description:
What if a child can scroll faster than they can read?

In this thought provoking talk, Kiona Nalendra explores why reading, writing, counting and basic knowledge still matter in an age of smartphones, social media and artificial intelligence.

Drawing on examples from Albert Einstein and Michael Faraday, personal experience and the Japanese reading aloud technique Ondoku, Kiona argues that foundational skills are not outdated or insignificant they are the roots that allow future learning and success to grow. 

Through a personal and emotional perspective, she challenges us to reconsider what children may be losing as technology continues to move forward.

 Kiona Madeline Nalendra is an 11 year old student at Avicenna Cinere Elementary School with a passion for literature, design, art, music, and languages. description: In the winter of 2009, Biren Parikh landed in Changchun, China, at minus 25 degrees Celsius, to face a demotivated team, a lone translator and a list of 38 critical issues on his company's first project in the country, one it could not afford to fail. He traces what carried him through back to 1992, when he failed to secure admission to an engineering college and his father stood by him. Drawing on project turnarounds from Manila to Changchun, marathon running and learning to speak in public as an introvert, he argues that grit is not a personality trait but a habit built one ordinary day at a time. With years of experience shaping businesses and backing promising startups, he brings a unique perspective on building companies, spotting opportunities, and creating long-term value in finance & innovation. description: Born with underdeveloped lungs and written off as a failure at school, Arjun Vajpai stood on the summit of Mount Everest at the age of 16, on an expedition funded by more than 24,000 ordinary Indians. Drawing on eighteen expeditions to the world's highest peaks, including four attempts on Makalu, paralysis at 7,100 metres and a stroke on Dhaulagiri, he shares three lessons the mountains taught him: never underestimate the power of a dream, make failure your closest companion, and meet every challenge through preparation, adaptation and steady forward movement. Everyone, he argues, has an Everest of their own to climb An elite Indian mountaineer, author, and explorer. At age 16, Arjun became one of the youngest Indians to scale Mount Everest. He is the first Indian man to summit eight of the world’s 14 highest peaks, redefining human endurance against career-threatening paralysis and extreme adversity. title: Find the Everest of Your Life  | Arjun Vajpai | TEDxIIM Nagpur

description: In this talk, I share the story behind one of my most memorable at the Golden Hall in Vienna, its not about the applause or the spotlight, but the struggle that happened before I stepped onto the stage. After my luggage was lost just days before the concert, I faced exhaustion, frustration, uncertainty, and countless moments when I wanted to give up. Through that experience, and through the many wrong notes and lonely hours of practice, I realized that success is not about being perfect. It is about continuing when no one is watching, learning from mistakes, and allowing difficult moments to shape who we become. Quennel Zhao is a student who spends much of his time at the piano, working through long hours of practice, repetition, and moments when progress feels slow or uncertain. He has performed in concerts and competitions, but what matters most to him is not the spotlight, but the process that leads up to it. Drawing on Stephen Hawking's story and her work with more than 5,000 neurodiverse individuals and their families, she distinguishes speech, language, and communication, and shows how tools such as PECS, sign language, and AAC offer different pathways to being heard. The talk invites audiences to move from awareness to advocacy to inclusion, and to stop mistaking silence for emptiness.
